name: Rename Legitimate Utilities
description: Adversaries may rename legitimate / system utilities to try to evade security mechanisms concerning the usage of those utilities. Security monitoring and control mechanisms may be in place for legitimate utilities adversaries are capable of abusing, including both built-in binaries and tools such as PSExec, AutoHotKey, and IronPython.(Citation: LOLBAS Main Site)(Citation: Huntress Python Malware 2025)(Citation: The DFIR Report AutoHotKey 2023)(Citation: Splunk Detect Renamed PSExec) It may be possible to bypass those security mechanisms by renaming the utility prior to utilization (ex: rename rundll32.exe).(Citation: Elastic Masquerade Ball) An alternative case occurs when a legitimate utility is copied or moved to a different directory and renamed to avoid detections based on these utilities executing from non-standard paths.(Citation: F-Secure CozyDuke)

telemetry.name: Command Execution
telemetry.description: Execution of a command and its interpreter or parent context.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect process command lines and relevant shell/interpreter audit; shell history alone is neither complete nor tamper-resistant.

providers.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
providers.scope: Script content via event 4104 when configured; channel depends on PowerShell edition.

providers.name: Sysmon process events
providers.scope: Interpreter launch and parent context, not full script content.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: execve-family execution context; shell built-ins need additional instrumentation.

configuration: Enable Script Block Logging through the policy/configuration for the installed edition. Forward Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational for Windows PowerShell, or PowerShellCore/Operational for PowerShell 7.
Retain script-block ID and fragment ordering alongside process creation. Protect access to collected script text; secrets may be included.
On Linux, use narrowly scoped Audit execution rules for the lab account and supported architectures, and retain joined SYSCALL/EXECVE/PATH records.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Script content and process command lines are different signals. Logging may be partial, fragmented, filtered or disabled; never assume a command line reveals everything executed.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per host role and principal: rare interpreters, command argument patterns and parent-child sequences. Normalize scripts carefully; obfuscation, administrative automation and missing command lines change visibility.

telemetry.name: File Creation
telemetry.description: Creation or overwrite of a file at an observed path.
telemetry.collection_focus: Scope Sysmon FileCreate (11) to the lab directory; retain the process and file path. Differentiate creation/overwrite if the sensor can.

providers.name: Microsoft Sysmon
providers.scope: Windows event-based collection; enable the event types needed below.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: Linux alternative for supported system-call and file events; different semantics and fields.

providers.name: Apple Endpoint Security clients
providers.scope: macOS alternative where the subscribed event exists; requires an entitled, approved client, not an iOS collector.

configuration: On a disposable Windows host, review the installed Sysmon schema and current configuration; merge scoped event filters into the existing policy rather than replacing it.
Forward Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational to the lab collector. Preserve event ID, timestamp, computer, process identifiers and the original event.
For Linux or macOS, select the equivalent sensor separately and test its emitted fields; a Windows event ID does not transfer across platforms.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Event filtering and sensor versions change coverage. High-volume image-load and process-access collection needs tuning; endpoint events alone do not establish intent.

telemetry.name: File Metadata
telemetry.description: File attributes such as path, size, timestamps, ownership and cryptographic hash.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect scoped file inventory/FIM metadata with hash algorithm and observation time; preserve original timestamps separately from collector time.

providers.name: osquery
providers.scope: Scheduled host-state queries; supported tables and privileges vary by OS. Select a table that actually exposes the required object.

providers.name: Linux Audit plus inventory snapshots
providers.scope: Events explain changes; snapshots describe state at collection time.

configuration: Define the inventory query, allowed host set, interval and least-privileged reader. Store a stable asset ID, observation time and collector version.
Keep successive snapshots and calculate additions, removals and changed attributes. Pair state changes with audit events when available.
Export collector health and missed-poll counts so a missing snapshot is not misclassified as a missing asset.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Snapshots miss short-lived objects and do not identify who caused a change. A generic inventory agent is not guaranteed to expose firmware or kernel-level details.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Compare authorized state snapshots: first-seen drivers/services/modules, unexpected configuration drift and integrity changes. Record collection cadence; absence in a sample is not evidence of deletion.

telemetry.collection_focus: Use file-integrity monitoring or scoped OS file-write auditing for general changes. Sysmon 2 records creation-time changes; it is not a general file-write event.

strategies.name: Renamed Legitimate Utility Execution with Metadata Mismatch and Suspicious Path

analytics.name: Analytic 0012
analytics.guidance: Execution of binaries where the on-disk filename does not match PE metadata such as OriginalFilename or InternalName. Often observed with renamed LOLBAS or system binaries like rundll32, powershell, or psexec.

tuning.description: Filter by suspicious or non-standard directory paths
Enable tuning based on mismatch rules between metadata and disk filename
Flag unusual or rare argument combinations for LOLBAS-like tools

analytics.name: Analytic 0013
analytics.guidance: Execution of renamed or relocated native macOS utilities with uncommon names or non-default paths (e.g., renamed `osascript`, `bash`, or `curl`).

tuning.description: Path deviation from expected directory (e.g., /usr/bin/ vs /tmp/)
Enable tuning based on hash matching known signed versions vs suspicious clones
Scope detections based on non-admin users using admin-level tools

analytics.name: Analytic 0014
analytics.guidance: Execution of renamed common utilities (e.g., `bash`, `nc`, `python`, `sh`) from atypical directories or with names intended to deceive defenders or EDRs.

tuning.description: Path anomalies such as execution from /dev/shm, /tmp, or user home directories
Unusual lineage such as scripts invoking renamed tools
Correlate between file rename and immediate execution

software.name: CozyCar
software.description: The [CozyCar](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0046) dropper has masqueraded a copy of the infected system's rundll32.exe executable that was moved to the malware's install directory and renamed according to a predefined configuration file.(Citation: F-Secure CozyDuke)

references.description: F-Secure Labs. (2015, April 22). CozyDuke: Malware Analysis. Retrieved December 10, 2015.

software.name: Kevin
software.description: [Kevin](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1020) has renamed an image of `cmd.exe` with a random name followed by a `.tmpl` extension.(Citation: Kaspersky Lyceum October 2021)

references.description: Kayal, A. et al. (2021, October). LYCEUM REBORN: COUNTERINTELLIGENCE IN THE MIDDLE EAST. Retrieved June 14, 2022.

software.name: DarkGate
software.description: [DarkGate](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1111) executes a Windows Batch script during installation that creases a randomly-named directory in the C:\\ root directory that copies and renames the legitimate Windows curl command to this new location.(Citation: Trellix Darkgate 2023)

references.description: Ernesto Fernández Provecho, Pham Duy Phuc, Ciana Driscoll & Vinoo Thomas. (2023, November 21). The Continued Evolution of the DarkGate Malware-as-a-Service. Retrieved February 9, 2024.

software.name: StrelaStealer
software.description: [StrelaStealer](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1183) has used a renamed, legitimate `msinfo32.exe` executable to sideload the [StrelaStealer](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1183) payload during initial installation.(Citation: DCSO StrelaStealer 2022)

references.description: DCSO CyTec Blog. (2022, November 8). #ShortAndMalicious: StrelaStealer aims for mail credentials. Retrieved December 31, 2024.

software.name: PHASEJAM
software.description: [PHASEJAM](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S9014) has renamed the file `/home/bin/remotedebug` to `remotedebug.bak`, allowing the threats actors to write a malicious `/home/bin/remotedebug` shell script.(Citation: Google UNC5221 Ivanti January 2025)

references.description: John Wolfram, Josh Murchie, Matt Lin, Daniel Ainsworth, Robert Wallace, Dimiter Andonov, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, Jacob Thompson. (2025, January 8). Ivanti Connect Secure VPN Targeted in New Zero-Day Exploitation. Retrieved April 14, 2026.

actors.name: Lazarus Group
actors.description: [Lazarus Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032) has renamed system utilities such as wscript.exe and mshta.exe.(Citation: Qualys LolZarus)

references.description: Pradhan, A. (2022, February 8). LolZarus: Lazarus Group Incorporating Lolbins into Campaigns. Retrieved March 22, 2022.

actors.name: menuPass
actors.description: [menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045) has renamed [certutil](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0160) and moved it to a different location on the system to avoid detection based on use of the tool.(Citation: FireEye APT10 Sept 2018)

references.description: Matsuda, A., Muhammad I. (2018, September 13). APT10 Targeting Japanese Corporations Using Updated TTPs. Retrieved September 17, 2018.

actors.name: APT32
actors.description: [APT32](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050) has moved and renamed pubprn.vbs to a .txt file to avoid detection.(Citation: Twitter ItsReallyNick APT32 pubprn Masquerade)

references.description: Carr, N.. (2017, December 26). Nick Carr Status Update APT32 pubprn. Retrieved September 12, 2024.

actors.name: APT38
actors.description: [APT38](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0082) has renamed system utilities, such as `rundll32.exe` and `mshta.exe`, to avoid detection.(Citation: 1 - appv)

references.description: SEONGSU PARK. (2022, December 27). BlueNoroff introduces new methods bypassing MoTW. Retrieved February 6, 2024.

actors.name: GALLIUM
actors.description: [GALLIUM](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0093) used a renamed cmd.exe file to evade detection.(Citation: Cybereason Soft Cell June 2019)

references.description: Cybereason Nocturnus. (2019, June 25). Operation Soft Cell: A Worldwide Campaign Against Telecommunications Providers. Retrieved July 18, 2019.

actors.name: Daggerfly
actors.description: [Daggerfly](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1034) used a renamed version of rundll32.exe, such as "dbengin.exe" located in the `ProgramData\Microsoft\PlayReady` directory, to proxy malicious DLL execution.(Citation: Symantec Daggerfly 2023)

references.description: Threat Hunter Team. (2023, April 20). Daggerfly: APT Actor Targets Telecoms Company in Africa. Retrieved July 25, 2024.

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.description: Use file system access controls to protect folders such as `C:\Windows\System32`.

candidates.name: Masquerading - wscript.exe running as svchost.exe
candidates.description:
Copies wscript.exe, renames it, and launches it to masquerade as an instance of svchost.exe.

Upon execution, no windows will remain open but wscript will have been renamed to svchost and ran out of the temp folder

dependencies.description: Wscript file to execute must exist on disk

candidates.name: Masquerading - cscript.exe running as notepad.exe
candidates.description:
Copies cscript.exe, renames it, and launches it to masquerade as an instance of notepad.exe.

Upon successful execution, cscript.exe is renamed as notepad.exe and executed from non-standard path.

candidates.name: Masquerading as Windows LSASS process
candidates.description:
Copies cmd.exe, renames it, and launches it to masquerade as an instance of lsass.exe.

Upon execution, cmd will be launched by powershell. If using Invoke-AtomicTest, The test will hang until the 120 second timeout cancels the session

candidates.name: Malicious process Masquerading as LSM.exe
candidates.description:
Detect LSM running from an incorrect directory and an incorrect service account
This works by copying cmd.exe to a file, naming it lsm.exe, then copying a file to the C:\ folder.

Upon successful execution, cmd.exe will be renamed as lsm.exe and executed from non-standard path.

candidates.name: Masquerading as FreeBSD or Linux crond process.
candidates.description:
Copies sh process, renames it as crond, and executes it to masquerade as the cron daemon.

Upon successful execution, sh is renamed to `crond` and executed.

candidates.name: Masquerading - powershell.exe running as taskhostw.exe
candidates.description:
Copies powershell.exe, renames it, and launches it to masquerade as an instance of taskhostw.exe.

Upon successful execution, powershell.exe is renamed as taskhostw.exe and executed from non-standard path.

candidates.name: Masquerading - non-windows exe running as windows exe
candidates.description:
Copies an exe, renames it as a windows exe, and launches it to masquerade as a real windows exe

Upon successful execution, powershell will execute T1036.003.exe as svchost.exe from on a non-standard path.

dependencies.description: Exe file to copy must exist on disk at specified location (#{inputfile})

candidates.name: Masquerading - windows exe running as different windows exe
candidates.description: Copies a windows exe, renames it as another windows exe, and launches it to masquerade as second windows exe

simulation.prerequisites: Use disposable lab hosts and test accounts, explicit target allowlists, a clean snapshot, bounded egress and a restore plan. Review every candidate and dependency before any execution.

synthetic.purpose: Collection/parser contract exercise, NOT a positive example or detection of this TTP.
